text: hru-web01, the public outage-reporting portal, and hru-db01, its backend database, get Lesson 2's Linux checklist applied -- but one sits directly on the internet and the other only talks to it internally, and that difference shapes how tightly each server's rules get scoped.

First, SSH, hardened carefully. PermitRootLogin no forces anyone needing root to log in as a named user first, and AllowUsers limits who can connect at all, even with a valid key. The safe order matters most: confirm key login works in a second, still-open session, check syntax, restart sshd, then verify a brand-new session before closing the originals -- never flip PasswordAuthentication to no and restart from your only open session.

Second, fail2ban stays enabled on both servers even with keys-only SSH. It's defense in depth -- a future misconfiguration that silently re-enables password auth is far less dangerous if fail2ban is already watching, banning any IP with five failed attempts in ten minutes for an hour.

Third, automatic security updates. hru-web01 sits directly on the internet, making it the server most likely to actually face exploitation of a known vulnerability if patching lags. Unattended-upgrades applies security patches automatically on both servers, instead of waiting on a manual cycle.

Fourth, ufw, scoped differently per server. hru-web01 opens SSH, HTTP, and HTTPS -- everything a public portal needs. hru-db01 opens SSH and its database port, but only from hru-web01's specific internal address, not the whole internal network.
With both operating systems hardened and verified, next lesson moves to the detection side -- writing Hartwell's first Microsoft Sentinel analytics rule.
